nameStory: Motherwort earned its name from centuries of use by mothers and midwives, who believed this herb helped with childbirth and women's health issues. The scientific name 'cardiaca' refers to its traditional use for heart ailments, while 'Leonurus' means 'lion's tail' in Latin, describing the plant's fuzzy, tapering flower spikes.
description: Common motherwort is a sturdy, square-stemmed perennial herb that belongs to the mint family. It grows 2-4 feet tall with deeply lobed, palm-shaped leaves that get smaller as they go up the stem. The plant produces small pink or white flowers in dense clusters around the stem, creating a distinctive tiered look. Originally from Asia and Europe, it has naturalized widely across New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive palm-shaped leaves with 3-5 deep lobes that feel slightly fuzzy and have a bitter, medicinal smell when crushed. Lower leaves are larger (2-4 inches) while upper leaves become much smaller and less divided.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink, purple, or white tubular flowers cluster in dense whorls around the square stem at each leaf joint, creating a stacked appearance like nature's layer cake. Flowers are fuzzy and have a two-lipped shape typical of the mint family.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in an upright, branching pattern with a distinctly square, hollow stem that's characteristic of mint family plants. The stem feels ridged when you roll it between your fingers.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, hard, three-sided nutlets that remain in the dried flower clusters through winter, creating spiky, persistent seed heads that rattle when shaken.

habitat: Look for motherwort in disturbed soils around old farmsteads, garden edges, roadsides, and waste places throughout New England. It thrives in rich, well-drained soil and often grows near stone walls, barnyards, and abandoned homesites where it was once cultivated. You'll frequently find it mixed with other weedy plants like nettle and burdock.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as distinctive palm-shaped leaves from the base, making identification easier before other plants leaf out fully.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from June through August in dense whorls around the stem. This is prime identification time when both flowers and full leaf development are visible.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to look scraggly as leaves yellow and drop, but the characteristic square stems and seed clusters remain visible.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems persist with spiky seed heads still attached, creating distinctive brown stalks that rattle in the wind and help identify old patches.

funFact: Motherwort is so hardy that it can live for decades in the same spot - some patches around old New England farmhouses are likely over 100 years old, descendants of plants grown by generations of farm wives who relied on it as their household medicine chest.
confusionNotes: Beginning plant enthusiasts often mistake young motherwort for other mint family plants, but the deeply palm-lobed leaves are the giveaway - most other mints have simple, unlobed leaves with just toothed edges.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this plant's common names with other species - 'lion's ear' and 'lion's tail' are also used for completely different plants in the genus Leonotis. When discussing motherwort, it's clearest to use the full name 'common motherwort' to avoid mix-ups.
compareHints: Common motherwort differs from its relative Chinese motherwort by having more deeply divided palm-shaped leaves, while Chinese motherwort has less divided, more oval leaves. Among other mint family plants in New England, motherwort's palm-lobed leaves make it quite distinctive - most other mints like spearmint or catnip have simple leaves with just toothed margins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Chinese motherwort is easily distinguished from its relative common motherwort by its much more finely divided leaves that look almost fern-like.
